1:
Whether Esau came as an enemy is the first question, and Clarke attacks the common answer at length. There is no kind of evidence of hostility, he says, no proof that the four hundred men were armed at all, and every proof that Esau behaved toward his brother with openness and candour and with a forgetfulness of past injuries of which only a great mind is capable; he asks why the man's character should be perpetually vilified, and answers that it serves a system in which Esau must be a reprobate and therefore everything bad. Calvin takes the opposite view and keeps Jacob's fear reasonable: his brother had still the same cause of hatred as before, and it was not probable that after leaving his father's house and living as he pleased he had grown milder, so that terror was not merely renewed but increased. Henry finds a third thing in the lifting of the eyes, reading it as cheerfulness rather than dejection, since one who has cast his care upon God may look before him with composure; Gill reports the same reading while allowing the act may have been simple watchfulness.

The ordering of the family is read as deliberate by everyone and charged against Jacob by two. Calvin takes it as prudence under danger, the wives and children placed so that if Esau attempted anything hostile the whole seed should not perish but part have time for flight; yet he will not defend the placing of Rachel and Joseph last, since the substance of the benediction lay in Judah, and though Jacob is excused because that oracle had not yet been revealed, Calvin says plainly that he was excessively indulgent to Rachel. Clarke puts two motives as alternatives and does not choose: either Jacob was still apprehensive and set foremost those he least esteemed, so that if the front met with evil the rest might escape on swift beasts, or he kept his choicest treasure to the last and showed Rachel and Joseph only after Esau had seen all the others, to make the deeper impression. Gill states the same order without the charge, that the handmaids went first as being less honourable and less beloved. Henry contrasts the brothers instead, Esau with a guard of four hundred looking big and Jacob followed by a cumbersome train of women and children.

Who receives the sevenfold obeisance is disputed on the page itself. Calvin argues that Jacob was not simply honouring his brother but worshipping God, partly in thanks and partly to implore him to make Esau propitious, and rests the case on the sequence, since the bowing is said to have been done seven times before he came near, so that the token of reverence was given before Esau was even in sight. His own editor prints a rebuttal underneath: those who think God was worshipped here do not say by what argument they prove it, since everything before and after indicates reverence shown to the brother, the handmaids and their sons bowing in the same words, and Leah, and last Rachel with Joseph; the conclusion offered is that this was civil reverence, which took nothing from the spiritual prerogative of the covenant. Ellicott takes the plain sense and adds the reason it was needed, that the quarrel had begun in Jacob's usurpation of the right of precedence, and describes the gesture as bending the body forward with the arms crossed and the right hand held over the heart. Wesley records only that he feared Esau as an enemy and did obeisance to him as an elder brother.
4:
The scribal marks over the word for kissing carry opposite meanings for two commentators. Clarke reports that in the Masoretic Bibles each letter of it is dotted to make it emphatic, and takes the rabbis to have meant by that notation to draw attention to the change in Esau and the sincerity with which he received his brother. Ellicott reports the same extraordinary pointing and the opposite intention, that the Masorites are supposed to have signified thereby that the kiss was not a sign of genuine love, and says roundly that for such an ill-natured supposition there is no warrant whatsoever. On the meeting itself the two agree. Clarke calls the conduct sincere, genuine and magnanimous, since Esau had buried all his resentment and forgotten his injuries; Ellicott holds that whatever his intention when he set out, the sight of his brother brought back the old times of their childhood, and that he never afterwards seems to have wavered in fraternal affection, being a man of warm feelings overmastered by loving impulses as he had been once before. Gill notes he would have alighted from whatever he rode to make haste, like the father of the prodigal.

Why Esau softened is answered by both Calvin and Wesley from providence rather than from character. Calvin makes it the effect of special favour, God proving by this method that he has the hearts of men in his hand, to soften their hardness and mitigate their cruelty when he pleases, taming them as wild beasts are tamed; and he bids us resort to that sacred anchor whenever the threats of enemies alarm us. He then distinguishes two ways the thing may work, since God does not always incline cruel minds to humanity but sometimes merely restrains them from harm while they rage; and he allows that Esau's malice may have been under constraint with the feeling of humanity gaining a temporary ascendancy, comparing the Egyptians who were driven to a moment's humanity while being nothing better than before, as the madness that soon broke out bore witness. Wesley says the same in a sentence, that God can of a sudden convert enemies into friends, and offers two men of the same name as instances, one changed by restraining grace and the other by renewing grace. On the tears he divides the causes, Jacob weeping for joy at the reception and Esau perhaps for shame at the design he had conceived.

Esau's question about the women and children draws out the passage's one piece of theology. Ellicott renders the Hebrew literally as who are these belonging to thee, and takes it for a request for fuller information about a family Esau could see was Jacob's. Henry observes that the account Jacob had sent ahead of the increase of his estate had said nothing of children, perhaps so as not to expose them to his brother's rage if he came as an enemy, or to please him with the unexpected sight if he came as a friend, so that the question was a natural one; and he notices that a sufficient answer would have been that they were his children, whereas the answer actually given calls them the children God has graciously given, which he takes as two claims at once, that they are God's gifts and that they are choice gifts, accounted great blessings though many and as yet slenderly provided for. Calvin draws the same confession out: children are not so produced by nature as to overturn the declaration that the fruit of the womb is a reward, since if the fecundity of brute animals is God's gift much more is that of men made in his image.
8:
Esau's question is taken by everyone as rhetorical rather than ignorant. Gill and Calvin both note that the drovers had already told him what the droves were for, so the enquiry was a way of declining, since when a thing does not please us we are apt to ask about it as though it were unknown. Ellicott adds a lexical observation instead, that the word Esau uses is the one for an encampment of pastoral people with their flocks, the same word rendered bands and company in the previous chapter and current in the narrative ever since Mahanaim; he suggests the five droves would have reminded Esau of cattle driven in at evening to their night quarters. Clarke supplies the custom that makes the exchange intelligible: in eastern countries a present received by a superior is a pledge of friendship and a present refused leaves everything to be feared, so Jacob was urgent precisely because acceptance would oblige Esau to treat him as a friend thereafter. Ellicott reads Esau's refusal as generosity rather than coldness, since he wished to spare his brother so large a gift and was himself rich.

The comparison of Esau's face to the face of God is the hardest phrase here, and three answers are given. Calvin raises the objection himself, that Jacob seems to wrong God by comparing him with a reprobate man, and to speak falsely besides, since given the choice he would have avoided this meeting altogether; he unties both knots by the Hebrew habit of calling whatever is excellent divine, and by observing that Esau thus changed was no obscure figure of God's favour. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same place by a different route, that Jacob might say it without cringing because he must have discerned God's work in the unexpected change of disposition and seen in his brother's friendliness a reflection of the divine. Ellicott grants there is much oriental hyperbole in it while insisting the comparison was not irreverent, since to the Hebrew the thought of God was not terrifying and the vision of his face was the sight of something good, God being nearer to men in those simple days than now that science has revealed the immensity of his attributes; what the phrase conveys is that Esau used his power as generously as God is wont to use his. Wesley reduces it to reconciliation.

Calling the present a blessing is glossed three ways. Calvin allows the noun to be taken actively or passively: actively it means accept the present by which I testify my goodwill, passively it refers the thing to God, so that what the Lord has bestowed by grace is liberally imparted in order that the brother may be in some measure a partaker of the same divine blessing. He prefers not to insist on the word, since Jacob immediately avows that what he possesses is not the fruit of his labour or industry but received through grace, and uses that as the argument for acceptance — the Lord has poured out abundance, of which some part may overflow without loss. Calvin then turns it on the reader, that nearly the same words are on all tongues while few truly ascribe to God what they possess, the greater part sacrificing to their own industry and scarcely one in a hundred convinced that whatever is good flows from gratuitous favour. Keil and Delitzsch keep the sense narrow, that the word means the present as expressive of a desire to bless, and that the claim to have all rather than merely much is made as heir of the divine promise. Ellicott adds that a gift was thought lucky and God the giver of all good luck.
12:
The grounds of the refusal are treated as practical and sufficient. Keil and Delitzsch explain the difficulty exactly: the flocks and herds are those giving milk, which is why they are an object of especial anxiety, and a caravan with delicate children and cattle needing care could not keep pace with a company of horsemen without taking harm, so that overdriving them a single day would kill the sheep. Ellicott corrects the rendering of the clause about pace, which is literally the foot of the cattle and of the children, and notes that Joseph was only six or seven while Leah's younger sons were too tender for much fatigue; Gill gives the range as thirteen down to about six and observes that Esau could see their stature. Ellicott also reports an inference drawn from the phrase about flocks that give suck, that the season was winter, which some think confirmed by Jacob afterwards making folds at Succoth; but he calls the conclusion uncertain and suggests Jacob halted there rather because of his lameness.

Whether Jacob meant what he said about following to Seir divides the page sharply, and Calvin stands alone against everyone else. He allows the reasons alleged are true but holds they are introduced under false pretexts, since Jacob afterwards turned his journey in another direction, so that he promised what he was not intending to do; and he presses the principle hard, that truth is so precious to God that he will not allow us to lie or deceive even when no injury follows. Calvin's own editor prints the rebuttal beneath: there is no reason to doubt Jacob said what he meant, he may have had other reasons for avoiding close intercourse with a man uninfluenced by religion, it is by no means certain he never went to Seir though he would have gone without his wives and flocks, and the silence of the sacred writers proves neither that he failed to go nor that he did not intend to, which is all that sincerity required. Clarke supposes him perfectly sincere and prevented afterwards by circumstances; Wesley presumes the visit was made once his concerns were settled though it is not recorded; Ellicott thinks it went uncarried out because Esau had not yet settled there.

On the escort declined, the commentators divide over how much caution to allow. Gill supposes the men were offered to show the way, to guard the road, and to make Jacob appear the more honourable on entering Seir. Keil and Delitzsch deny any distrust in the refusal and insist the ground given was no mere pretext, since a military guard was unnecessary to a man who knew himself defended by the hosts of God. Wesley says the same and turns it into a rule, that those are sufficiently guarded who have God for their guard, adding that the closing words mean Jacob wanted nothing from his brother but his favour. Calvin will not let the caution pass so easily. He grants that Jacob feared no perfidy hidden under the garb of friendship but was avoiding fresh occasions of offence, since a proud man may be exasperated again by light causes; and yet he dares not deny that the anxiety was excessive, asking whence such an incredible change of mind in Esau could have come unless he had been divinely transformed from a wolf into a lamb, and drawing the lesson that we should restrain our anxieties rather than tremble over an affair God has already provided for.
16:
Where Succoth stood is settled by two arguments. Keil and Delitzsch reason from the next verse, that since Jacob crossed a ford of the Jordan after leaving it, Succoth cannot have belonged to Canaan and must lie on the eastern side. Ellicott weighs two claimants: one in the tribe of Gad east of the river, in the corner formed by the Jordan and the Jabbok, and another still called Sakut on the western bank, which he rejects because it lies ten miles north of the junction and Jacob would hardly go so far out of his way. Gill agrees on the eastern site, placing it in a valley within the territory of Sihon king of Heshbon and afterwards allotted to Gad, mentioned in company with Penuel and reported only two miles from it, a distance he thinks too short. Both Gill and Calvin note that the name is used here by anticipation, since no city yet stood there; the place took its name from what Jacob did.

Ellicott finds the building itself remarkable and makes an argument out of it. Cattle in that country remain in the open air the whole year round, so that making folds for them is quite unusual, and the fact that the spot kept the name of the booths shows the thing was noticed at the time; he treats this as a strong though undesigned testimony to the truth of the narrative. He then reconstructs why Jacob stopped. Pursued by Laban, he had suffered much from anxiety and from the labour of a hurried removal; delivered from the danger behind he had to face a greater danger in front and passed many days and nights in terror; having done everything a man could do he stayed behind to recover himself, and instead of a few restful hours wrestled fiercely all night and found at sunrise that his hip was sprained; he got through the interview with his brother agitated by turns with fear and hope and joy while enduring the pain as best he could, and then, the danger over, he broke down. On this reading the word journeyed means only that he shifted camp from the high ground into the corner close by, where two rivers would protect him and water his cattle.

Why the name was given at all is answered by Calvin from the man's history rather than from the structures. Jacob had found no quiet resting-place until he came there, and so he fixed the memorial of divine grace on this spot and no other, though he had pitched tents in many places along the way, because here at length it was granted him to remain in some abode and he had not dared before to plant his foot firmly anywhere. Clarke reads the stay as a long one, supposing the family in all probability continued there for a considerable time. Henry turns the name forward into the nation's memory: the place afterwards became a city beyond Jordan in the tribe of Gad, and its name means booths, so that when his posterity came to dwell in houses of stone they might remember that a Syrian ready to perish was their father, a man glad of booths, that being the rock from which they were hewn. Gill adds only that Esau took his leave the same day he met his brother and set out for Seir, though whether he arrived within the day is uncertain and the journey was probably longer than that.
18:
Whether Shalem is a place or an adjective is nearly settled, and the near-unanimity is worth noting. Clarke holds it should be rendered in peace or in safety and is unlikely to be a city name, being found nowhere else, citing Coverdale and Matthews for that translation with the Chaldee and the Arabic agreeing. Wesley renders it he came safe. Keil and Delitzsch call it an adjective meaning safe or peaceful, equivalent to the phrase in the Bethel vow, and draw the conclusion that gives the verse its weight: what Jacob had asked for before leaving Canaan was now fulfilled, since he had returned in safety to the land. Ellicott refines the sense against the common rendering, since in peace would not mean peaceably but that his troubles were at an end and his lameness cured; he prefers a rendering meaning in good condition, and notes that Rashi likewise saw an allusion to the healing of the limp. Gill alone leans the other way, canvassing candidate towns and rejecting both Jerusalem as forty miles off and the Salem of Melchizedek, while reporting that the Jewish writers generally take the word of his coming in peace and health.

The purchase draws two observations and one long philological excursion. Gill notes that he bought a part of a field and not the whole, and that though heir of the country he bought at all because the time for possession was not yet come; Ellicott sets the transaction in a series, since Abraham a century earlier had been obliged to buy a burial place from an owner who could give him title, and Jacob must now buy even the ground on which to pitch his tent, which would have been required only in the immediate neighbourhood of a town. He adds that this first parcel is where the embalmed body of Joseph was afterwards buried, and finds it remarkable that possession of it stayed secure while the owners were far away in Egypt. On the price the two part company. Clarke reports that the word signifies a lamb, so that a hundred lambs may be meant, and canvasses the conjecture that the coin bore a lamb's figure and took its name from the stamp, illustrating from coins named for their images and from the Athenian ox. Ellicott holds the unit was plainly an ingot of some value, on the evidence of the Book of Job, and says flatly that for the rendering lambs there is no support.

The altar is read as three things at once. Ellicott lists them: a thankoffering for the safe return, a taking possession of the country, and chiefly a profession of faith, which is why the title given it could not be the covenant name but had to acknowledge the new name Jacob had just received, so that the man now called a prince with God confesses whose prince he is. Calvin is concerned rather with what an altar was for, warning the reader not to think the patriarchs trifled with worship: under the word he would have us understand the external testimony of piety, the offering of victims and invoking of the name by a pure rite handed down from Noah and Shem. He finds in it a measure of the man, that though broken down by various troubles he was not forgetful of the altar, and did not content himself with worshipping privately in the secret feeling of his mind, since men want helps while they are in the flesh; and he adds the domestic motive, that a pious father must take care his house is not profane but that God reigns in it as in a sanctuary. Clarke suggests rendering the name as the strong God is the God of Israel.
